Airbnb (ABNB) stock returned 50.7% over the past twelve months, against 12.8% for the S&P 500. The company continued to buy back its own shares during that time, and its diluted share count is 9.5% smaller than it was three years ago. This reduction means each share you own holds a larger slice of the business and its profits. So has that bigger slice come with bigger earnings for each share?

Airbnb’s diluted earnings per share fell 13.5% a year between the twelve months ended September 2023 and the twelve months ended September 2026. The company’s net income fell 16.3% a year over the same period. With fewer shares outstanding, each share’s earnings fell more slowly than the profit, but they still fell. The starting point was unusually high, though: the $5.46 billion profit in the twelve months ended September 2023 came on only $2.25 billion of operating income.

The whole fall came in the first of those three years, and per-share earnings have risen in each year since. In the twelve months ended September 2026, Airbnb’s earnings per share rose 27.1%, against 21.9% for its net income. This means each share’s slice grew faster than the profit behind it. The company spent $3.95 billion buying back shares over those twelve months, though the $1.77 billion it paid employees in stock offset part of that total. Net of that stock pay, Airbnb’s buybacks equaled 2.0% of its market value at the November 11, 2026 close.

Airbnb put its free cash flow over the twelve months ended September 2026 at $4.9 billion, more than it spent on buybacks. That cash comes from a booking business that grew faster than a year earlier. Revenue rose 16.7% to $13.9 billion over those same twelve months, and management said hotel bookings accelerated in fiscal Q3 2026.

Airbnb also holds far more cash than debt. The company ended September 2026 with $12.6 billion of cash and short-term investments, against $2.41 billion of debt. On November 5, 2026, management announced that the board had approved a new $12 billion repurchase program, which comes on top of what was left under the existing plan. That new program alone equals about 11% of the company’s $107 billion market value.

Thursday, Nov. 5, was one of the market’s roughest sessions in years. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52%, its worst day since April 2025, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 dropped 6.36%, its steepest decline since March 2020. Selling was driven in part by fears that Democrats’ midterm gains could slow the AI data center buildout, and chip stocks took the brunt, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF NASDAQ: SMH falling by roughly 11%.

Airbnb NASDAQ: ABNB didn’t escape entirely, slipping 3.5% to close at $170.13. But it held up far better than the broader tech market, and it was still up about 3.5% on the week and more than 25% year to date heading into its report. That relative strength made Airbnb's third-quarter earnings release even more interesting. Would the results justify the stock’s outperformance and notable relative strength, or give investors a reason to lock in gains?
At least initially, the answer was clear. Shares jumped about 11% in after-hours trading to trade near $189, within roughly 2% of their 52-week high of $193.45.

Airbnb’s third-quarter revenue rose 19% to $4.87 billion, its fastest growth in more than three years and well ahead of the roughly $4.75 billion analysts expected. Earnings of $3.16 per share also beat the $2.85 consensus by 31 cents, though a lower tax provision flattered the year-over-year comparison.

sum: Airbnb, the popular peer-to-peer home rental platform, has seen its stock surge in after-hours trading, buoyed by a robust performance in the third quarter and optimistic forecasts for the remainder of the year. The company’s CEO, Brian Chesky, celebrated the results, stating, “Airbnb is back in growth mode.” He highlighted the rarity of a marketplace of Airbnb’s magnitude reaccelerating growth, emphasizing the significant momentum the company is experiencing.

In its latest earnings report, Airbnb revealed earnings per share of $3.16, comfortably exceeding Wall Street’s estimated figures of $2.85 per share, as per S&P Global Market Intelligence data. The company’s revenue for the quarter reached $4.87 billion, representing a 19% increase and surpassing analyst expectations of $4.74 billion.

Airbnb reported particularly strong booking figures in North America, noting that nights booked had grown at their fastest pace in four years. The company also acknowledged a notable trend: not only are previous guests returning to the platform, but there is an increase in first-time users discovering the service.

The encouraging results prompted Airbnb to revise its guidance for the fourth quarter, predicting revenue growth of 16% to 19%, which translates to an estimated range of $3.22 billion to $3.28 billion. This forecast also exceeds the midpoint estimate of $3.16 billion projected by analysts. For the full fiscal year, Airbnb anticipates revenue growth in the high teens, alongside an expectation that adjusted EBITDA margins will rise to approximately 36%.

This strong performance underscores the resilience of Airbnb in the face of global travel demand, indicating a positive trajectory as the company continues to capitalize on market trends and consumer preferences.

That would represent an improvement from the 9.7 percent increase recorded in the same quarter last year. Analysts have broadly maintained their estimates over the past 30 days, pointing to expectations for continued execution rather than a major change in the operating outlook.

The key question for investors is whether booking growth remains the main driver of the business or whether the reported expansion depends more heavily on pricing and mix. The previous quarter's increase in nights booked provides a demanding reference point for the upcoming release. Airbnb's results will also show whether investment in product development and other growth initiatives is weighing on profitability as the company expands its platform.

Recent results from other consumer-internet companies provide an uneven backdrop. StockStory said Booking's revenue declined 1.3 percent year over year and missed analysts' expectations by 7 percent, while Fiverr's revenue fell 15.8 percent but exceeded expectations by 8.4 percent. These outcomes underline the importance of company-specific booking trends and guidance in Airbnb's release.

For a business that beat revenue estimates in each of the last five quarters and still runs a free-cash-flow margin near 37%, a market that suddenly wants to pay less deserves an answer: is this fear rational, or is it an opening?

When a name known for bullish coverage picks up a high-profile neutral voice, the marginal buyer hesitates. Paris is ground zero for Europe’s backlash against illegal Airbnbs
sum: Early one drizzly morning in Paris, a handful of city officials make their way up a steep, narrow street in the historic neighborhood of Montmartre, with a reporter in tow and the domed Sacré-Coeur basilica looming above. The group stops at an apartment building that looks like any other on the block. It is only when they step inside the entrance hall that anything seems unusual. Signs pasted to the walls declare that loud noise and nighttime gatherings are forbidden. And many of the front doors have metal lockboxes bolted to them, with apartment keys inside. Both are telltale signs that the city workers have found what they’re looking for: illegal Airbnbs.

During the next half-hour, as we climb stairs and knock on doors, a few sleepy residents emerge to complain—not about us, but to us. They describe how their building has begun to feel like a travelers’ crash pad, with rolling suitcases clattering on the pavestones at all hours, and the outdoor courtyard becoming a rowdy tavern on warm evenings. “A living hell,” one calls it.

These modest Montmartre homes are just one flash point in Europe’s growing Airbnb backlash. Even as short-term home rentals have become a global travel norm, more cities worldwide have blamed Airbnb and its competitors for their housing squeeze and affordability crises. In Europe, and in Paris in particular, the growing opposition has gathered real momentum. Paris’s restrictions are among the most rigid, sharply limiting the number of nights that any property can be made available for short-term rentals. The owners of those Montmartre apartments could face fines of well over €100,000 if it’s proved they have violated the law.

“People are buying up properties, becoming a kind of hotelier, developing these businesses that are taking apartments out of the local market,” outgoing Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo fumes over lunch in City Hall’s ornate dining room. Hidalgo, whose term expired in March, describes how she, together with the mayors of Barcelona and Rome, spent years pushing the 27-country European Union to crack down on Airbnb.

items.t: Spanish court orders Airbnb to pay €64 million fine and refuses to suspend sanction
sum: Madrid’s High Court refuses to suspend a €64 million fine on Airbnb by Spain’s Consumer Ministry for illegal holiday rentals and misleading ads; the platform must pay while it appeals.

Airbnb has suffered another setback in the Spanish market. On Monday, the High Court of Justice of Madrid (TSJM) rejected the company’s request for interim measures to suspend payment of the nearly €64 million fine imposed on it by the Ministry of Consumer Affairs in December 2025. As a result of this decision, the platform must pay the penalty while the court case continues.

The ruling does not go into the substance of the case, but simply rejects the company’s request to halt payment until a final judgment is issued. Airbnb, however, still intends to challenge the fine, arguing that it runs counter to the Spanish and European legal framework.

The fine was issued for a number of infringements linked to the publication of tourist accommodation adverts on its platform. Chief among them were the listing of unlicensed properties, the use of false or incorrect registration numbers and the lack of accurate information about hosts, practices that the authorities describe as misleading for consumers.

According to Spain’s Ministry of Consumer Affairs, the amount of the fine is equivalent to six times the illegal profit made through these practices. The irregularities also affected tens of thousands of adverts that breached the regional regulations in force on tourist accommodation.

The government has sought to tighten control over short-term tourist rentals in order to tackle the housing crisis affecting Spain and other major European markets. Other countries, including France, Italy and Portugal, have also toughened their rules in response to the impact on access to housing.

items.t: Airbnb's $2.5 Billion Bond Sale Surprises Market, Sending Shares Lower
sum: Airbnb (ABNB) shares fell sharply on Wednesday after the vacation rental giant announced a surprise $2.5 billion bond offering, a move that caught investors off guard and raised questions about the company's capital strategy. The stock dropped approximately 5% following a Bloomberg report detailing the new debt issuance.

The offering, which marks Airbnb's debut in the investment-grade bond market, consists of 3-, 5-, and 10-year notes. The sale was led by major financial institutions Bank of America (BAC), Goldman Sachs (GS), and Morgan Stanley (MS). The primary impetus for the fundraising is the impending maturity of $2 billion in 0% convertible senior notes on March 15, 2026.

Those zero-interest notes were issued in 2021 with a conversion price of $288.64 per share, a level far above the stock's current trading price. This made the conversion feature effectively worthless, leaving Airbnb with a straightforward $2 billion debt repayment obligation. The new bond sale is widely seen as a refinancing maneuver to address this maturity.

The market's negative reaction stemmed from several key factors. First and foremost, the company is transitioning from a cost-free debt structure to one that carries interest payments. The 2021 convertible notes carried a 0% coupon, providing Airbnb with exceptionally cheap capital during its post-IPO growth phase. The new bonds, while investment-grade, will introduce a recurring interest expense, signaling a rise in the company's overall cost of capital.

Secondly, Airbnb's strong liquidity position gave investors pause. The company holds over $11 billion in liquid assets, a substantial financial cushion. This led analysts and shareholders to question the immediate necessity of raising an additional $2.5 billion through debt, especially given the company's recent focus on reducing leverage and returning capital to shareholders via stock buybacks.

Finally, the unexpected nature of the sale sparked concerns about a potential shift in financial strategy. The move would nearly double Airbnb's current debt load, moving away from what many perceived as a capital-light, balance sheet-conservative approach that had been in place for the past few years.

items.t: Airbnb vs. Vrbo: Which Is Better for Travelers?
sum: Vacation rentals offer many potential benefits compared with hotel rooms, including lower prices, more amenities and a more personal touch. Yet knowing which vacation rental platform provides the best overall experience for travelers is another question.

There is a clear winner between Airbnb versus Vrbo: Airbnb. Our analysis found that Airbnb offers a better overall experience for most travelers. That said, the right booking platform for you will depend on your travel preferences.
The biggest difference between these two platforms is the type of accommodation they offer:
- Vrbo offers stand-alone vacation homes only. It doesn't generally offer “shared” spaces like private rooms or more unusual options like campsites.
- Airbnb offers stand-alone vacation homes as well as shared spaces and even hotel rooms. Although it started as a home-sharing concept, it now hosts many types of accommodations.

In other words, if you’re looking for a home to rent for a family get-together, both Airbnb and Vrbo are good choices. But if you’re looking for a cheaper shared space or something less typical, stick with Airbnb.

If you’ve had bad luck with vacation rentals in the past, which were dumpier or dirtier than the pictures suggested, you might consider searching for Airbnb “Plus” properties, which have been vetted in person for quality.
